title: Creatine Supplement for Teen Athletes: Is It Safe?

contentHtml:
Walk into any gym or sports nutrition store, and you're likely to see shelves lined with creatine supplements. Social media influencers praise it, elite athletes use it, and even teenagers are asking their parents if they should take it.

But is creatine really safe for teenagers?

As a sports nutritionist, this is one of the most common questions I hear from parents of young athletes. Some worry that creatine might damage their child's kidneys. Others wonder if it affects growth or hormones. Many don't know whether a teenager needs a supplement at all.

The good news is that creatine is one of the most researched sports supplements in the world. Hundreds of studies have examined its effectiveness and safety in adults, and emerging research has also looked at its use in adolescents. However, like any supplement, the answer isn't as simple as "everyone should take it" or "no teenager should ever use it."

The decision depends on factors such as age, training level, sporting goals, diet quality, and whether the basics of nutrition are already in place.

In this article, we'll explore what creatine is, how it works, whether it's safe for teen athletes, who may benefit from it, and what parents should know before making a decision.

Key Takeaways

  • Creatine is one of the most researched sports supplements available.
  • Creatine occurs naturally in foods such as meat and fish.
  • It may improve performance during repeated short, high-intensity exercise.
  • Current evidence suggests creatine monohydrate is generally safe for healthy adolescent athletes when used appropriately under professional guidance.
  • Creatine is not a shortcut for better performance. Good nutrition, adequate sleep, structured training, and recovery remain far more important.

What Is Creatine?

Despite being sold as a supplement, creatine is not an artificial chemical. It is a natural compound made from three amino acids, such as arginine, glycine, and methionine. Your liver, kidneys, and pancreas produce around one gram of creatine every day. Another gram usually comes from foods like meat and fish.

About 95% of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscles, while the remaining amount is found in the brain and other organs. Inside muscle cells, creatine is stored mainly as phosphocreatine, which acts like a rapidly available energy reserve during intense exercise.

Think of phosphocreatine as a rechargeable battery. During short bursts of activity such as sprinting, jumping, swimming, lifting weights, or throwing, your muscles need energy immediately. Phosphocreatine helps regenerate ATP, the body's immediate energy source. This allows the muscles to keep producing high power for a little longer.

This is why creatine is especially useful in sports involving repeated explosive efforts.

Creatine for Teen Athlete: How Does Creatine Improve Performance?

Every movement your body makes requires ATP (adenosine triphosphate). The problem is that your muscles only store enough ATP for a few seconds of maximum effort. Once these stores are used, performance begins to decline unless ATP can be regenerated quickly.

Creatine helps solve this problem.

By increasing phosphocreatine stores inside muscles, creatine enables faster ATP regeneration during repeated high-intensity efforts. This means athletes may be able to:

  • produce more power
  • sprint repeatedly with less fatigue
  • complete more repetitions during strength training
  • recover faster between short bursts of exercise
  • improve training quality over time

Rather than acting like a stimulant, creatine supports the body's natural energy system. The greatest improvements are usually seen over weeks or months because athletes can train harder and recover better—not because creatine produces an instant performance boost.

Which Sports Benefit Most from Creatine?

Creatine is most effective for activities that rely on repeated explosive movements.

Examples include:

  • Swimming (particularly sprint events)
  • Athletics (sprints, jumps, throws)
  • Football
  • Rugby
  • Hockey
  • Basketball
  • Volleyball
  • Tennis
  • Badminton
  • Wrestling
  • Martial arts
  • Weightlifting
  • Powerlifting
  • Sprint cycling

Athletes competing in endurance events such as marathon running generally experience much smaller benefits because their performance relies primarily on aerobic energy systems. Even within swimming, a 50-metre sprinter is more likely to benefit than someone training exclusively for long-distance open-water events.

Clinical Insight from My Practice as a Sports Nutritionist

Over the years, I've worked with competitive swimmers, racquet sport athletes, runners, and adolescent athletes preparing for state and national competitions. One pattern I see repeatedly is that many families start asking about creatine before addressing the fundamentals. Some athletes skip breakfast, don't eat enough carbohydrate around training, drink very little water during long practice sessions, or consistently fall short of their daily protein needs.

In these situations, improving everyday nutrition almost always has a much bigger impact than introducing a supplement. Creatine can be helpful for selected athletes, but it should be viewed as the final layer—not the foundation. The athletes who consistently perform at their best are those who first build strong habits around food, hydration, sleep, and recovery.

Can Teen Athletes Benefit from Creatine?

The short answer is yes. But not every teenager needs it. Most of the research on creatine has been conducted in adults. However, studies involving adolescent athletes suggest that creatine may improve:

  • maximal strength
  • repeated sprint performance
  • lean body mass
  • power output
  • training adaptations

These improvements appear to be greatest in teenagers who:

  • participate in structured training
  • compete regularly
  • perform high-intensity sports
  • have completed puberty or are in later stages of adolescence

Importantly, creatine does not replace hard work. A teenager who rarely trains, sleeps poorly, and eats an unbalanced diet is unlikely to see meaningful improvements simply by taking creatine. The supplement works best when combined with a well-designed training program and an overall healthy diet.

Can Food Provide Enough Creatine?

Many parents ask whether supplements are necessary if their child eats well. The answer depends partly on dietary habits. Foods naturally rich in creatine include:

  • Beef
  • Lamb
  • Pork
  • Chicken (smaller amounts)
  • Tuna
  • Salmon
  • Herring

However, cooking slightly reduces creatine content, and most teenagers consume only modest amounts from food. Vegetarian and vegan athletes often have lower muscle creatine stores because plant foods contain virtually no creatine. Research suggests these athletes may experience greater increases in muscle creatine after supplementation.

That said, this does not automatically mean every vegetarian teenager should take creatine. The decision should still be based on training demands, sporting goals, nutritional intake, and professional assessment.

Creatine for Teen Athlete: Is it Safe?

This is the question that concerns most parents—and understandably so. The internet is full of conflicting opinions. One website says creatine is completely safe, while another warns it could harm a teenager's kidneys or affect growth. Social media only adds to the confusion, with influencers promoting supplements without explaining who they are actually appropriate for.

So, what does the science say? The answer is reassuring. But, it also comes with important caveats. Based on the evidence available today, creatine monohydrate appears to be safe for healthy adolescent athletes when used appropriately under the guidance of a qualified healthcare professional or sports nutritionist. However, this does not mean every teenager should take it.

Unlike caffeine or many pre-workout supplements, creatine is not a stimulant. It is a naturally occurring compound that your body already produces and stores in muscles. Supplementation simply increases those muscle stores beyond what diet alone can usually provide.

Several professional organisations, including the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), recognise creatine monohydrate as one of the most effective and well-researched sports supplements available. While most research has been conducted in adults, studies involving adolescent athletes have not identified serious adverse effects when creatine is used responsibly in healthy individuals.

At the same time, experts agree that supplements should never be the first step in improving athletic performance. Young athletes should first establish consistent eating habits, adequate energy intake, sufficient protein, good sleep, structured training, and appropriate recovery.

What Do Professional Organisations Recommend?

Professional bodies take a balanced approach. They do not recommend creatine for every child or teenager, but they also do not conclude that it is inherently unsafe.

Instead, they emphasise that creatine may be considered when an adolescent athlete:

  • Participates in serious, structured training.
  • Has completed or is close to completing puberty.
  • Eats a balanced diet that already meets energy and nutrient needs.
  • Understands that supplements cannot replace training or healthy eating.
  • Uses only high-quality creatine monohydrate products.
  • Takes it under the supervision of a qualified healthcare professional or sports dietitian.

This cautious approach reflects the fact that adolescents are still growing, and long-term studies spanning many years remain limited.

Does Creatine Damage the Kidneys?

This is perhaps the biggest myth surrounding creatine. For healthy individuals with normal kidney function, current evidence does not show that recommended doses of creatine damage the kidneys. So why does this myth persist?

When someone takes creatine, blood levels of creatinine may increase slightly. Creatinine is a normal waste product formed when creatine is broken down. Doctors often measure creatinine as part of kidney function tests. Seeing a slightly higher creatinine level after creatine supplementation may be mistaken for kidney disease if the healthcare provider is unaware that the person is taking creatine.

In reality, this small increase often reflects greater creatine availability rather than kidney injury. However, this does not mean everyone should take creatine. Teenagers with existing kidney disease, reduced kidney function, or other significant medical conditions should avoid creatine unless advised by their treating physician.

Does Creatine Affect Growth or Puberty?

Parents often ask whether creatine could interfere with hormones, growth plates, or puberty. Fortunately, there is no evidence that creatine delays growth or disrupts normal puberty in healthy adolescents.

Creatine is not a hormone.

  • It does not increase testosterone.
  • It does not act like anabolic steroids.
  • It does not alter growth plates.

Many people confuse creatine with anabolic steroids because both are sometimes discussed together in sports. In reality, they are completely different substances with entirely different mechanisms of action.

Does Creatine Cause Hair Loss?

This concern became popular after a small study in rugby players reported an increase in dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone linked with male pattern hair loss. However, several important points are often overlooked.

The study did not show that participants actually lost hair. The increase in DHT has not been consistently replicated in later research. To date, there is no convincing evidence that creatine supplementation causes hair loss.

If someone has a strong genetic predisposition to male pattern baldness, researchers cannot completely rule out whether creatine might play a minor role, but current evidence is insufficient to conclude that creatine causes hair loss.

Does Creatine Cause Dehydration or Muscle Cramps?

Many coaches once believed that creatine increased dehydration, muscle cramps, or heat illness. Current research does not support these concerns. Interestingly, several studies suggest the opposite. Because creatine increases water stored inside muscle cells, it may actually improve hydration within the muscles rather than reduce it.

That does not mean athletes can ignore hydration. Teen athletes should still drink enough fluids before, during, and after training, particularly during hot and humid weather. Good hydration remains essential regardless of whether creatine is used.

Does Creatine Cause Weight Gain?

Yes, but not necessarily in the way many parents fear. During the first few weeks of supplementation, many athletes gain 0.5–2 kg. This usually happens because muscles store more water along with increased creatine.

It is not the same as gaining body fat. Over time, athletes who combine creatine with effective strength training may also develop more lean muscle mass. For athletes competing in weight-class sports such as wrestling or boxing, or aesthetic sports where body weight is closely monitored, this initial increase should be discussed with their coach and sports nutritionist.

Clinical Insight from My Practice as a Sports Nutritionist

One of the most common misconceptions I encounter is that supplements create elite athletes. In reality, I've worked with national-level swimmers and adolescent athletes who improved significantly without using creatine simply because they corrected chronic under-fuelling.

Skipping breakfast before early morning training, eating too little carbohydrate around workouts, inadequate protein intake, and poor hydration are far more common barriers to performance than a lack of creatine. On the other hand, I've also worked with older adolescent athletes competing at high levels whose nutrition, recovery, and training were already well optimised. In selected cases like these, creatine supplementation became one small piece of a much larger performance plan.

The difference is that the supplement came after the fundamentals, not before them.

Which Type of Creatine Is Best?

If a teenager is advised to take creatine, the answer is surprisingly simple. Creatine monohydrate remains the gold standard. Despite marketing claims, there is no consistent evidence that newer forms, such as creatine hydrochloride (HCl), buffered creatine, liquid creatine, or creatine ethyl ester, provide superior results.

Creatine monohydrate has been used in the overwhelming majority of scientific studies, making it the best-supported option for both effectiveness and safety. Choose a product that has been independently tested for quality and is free from banned substances, especially for athletes competing in organised sport.

Learn more about creatine loading and if it is required.

Should Teenagers Load Creatine?

Adults sometimes follow a loading protocol of around 20 grams per day for 5–7 days, followed by a lower maintenance dose. For adolescent athletes, this rapid loading phase is generally not necessary. A lower daily dose reaches the same muscle creatine levels over a few weeks while reducing the likelihood of stomach discomfort.

For most teen athletes, a simple once-daily dose is sufficient if supplementation is appropriate.

How Much Creatine Should Teen Athletes Take?

There is no universally accepted dosage specifically for adolescents. In practice, recommendations are usually individualised based on:

  • Age
  • Body size
  • Training load
  • Sporting demands
  • Overall dietary intake

Rather than copying advice from social media, teenagers should seek guidance from a qualified sports dietitian or sports nutritionist familiar with adolescent athletes.

Who Should Avoid Creatine?

Creatine is not appropriate for everyone. It should generally be avoided or only used under medical supervision in teenagers who have:

  • Kidney disease
  • Significant liver disease
  • Certain metabolic disorders
  • Unexplained kidney abnormalities
  • Medical conditions requiring specialist supervision

It is also unnecessary for children who are not participating in structured sport.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is creatine a steroid?

No. Creatine is a naturally occurring compound and has no relation to anabolic steroids.

Can a 14-year-old take creatine?

There is no single age at which creatine becomes appropriate. The decision depends more on biological maturity, training status, sporting level, and professional guidance than chronological age.

Does creatine improve endurance?

Not significantly. Creatine works best for repeated short, high-intensity efforts rather than prolonged endurance exercise.

Can vegetarian athletes benefit more?

Possibly. Because vegetarian diets contain little or no creatine, these athletes may experience larger increases in muscle creatine stores after supplementation.

Is creatine banned in sport?

No. Creatine is not prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).

The Bottom Line

Creatine is one of the most extensively studied sports supplements available, and current evidence suggests that creatine monohydrate can be a safe and effective option for some healthy adolescent athletes when used appropriately and under professional guidance.

However, it is not a magic solution, and it is certainly not a substitute for good nutrition, structured training, quality sleep, and adequate recovery.

As a sports nutritionist, I encourage parents to view creatine as the final 5%, not the first step. Before considering any supplement, make sure your teenager is consistently eating enough to fuel training, recovering well, staying hydrated, and meeting their daily protein and energy needs.
